'''Richard James Saykally''' (born September 10, 1947) is an American chemist and the Class of 1932 Endowed Professor of Chemistry at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], where he studies the [[molecular]] characteristics of [[water]] and aqueous solutions.<ref name="nas_profile">{{Cite web |title=Richard J. Saykally – NAS |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/richard-j-saykally-qtc620/ |publisher=[[National Academy of Sciences]] |access-date=2026-07-22}}</ref>

== Biography ==
Saykally was born in [[Rhinelander, Wisconsin]] and completed his undergraduate education at the [[University of Wisconsin-Eau Claire]].<ref name="rjsgrp">{{Cite web |title=Contact and Bio |url=https://www.cchem.berkeley.edu/~rjsgrp/contactandbio.php |publisher=Saykally Group, University of California, Berkeley |access-date=2026-07-22}}</ref> He received his PhD from the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]] under R. Claude Woods in 1977,<ref name="thesis">{{Cite web |title=Microwave spectroscopy of transient molecular species in glow discharges |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IWzTAAAAMAAJ |publisher=University of Wisconsin–Madison |date=1977}}</ref> then completed postgraduate research at the [[National Institute of Standards and Technology]] with Kenneth Melvin Evenson.<ref name="ucb_profile">{{Cite web |title=Richard J. Saykally |url=https://chemistry.berkeley.edu/people/richard-saykally |publisher=[[University of California, Berkeley]] |access-date=2026-07-22}}</ref> He joined the faculty at the University of California, Berkeley in 1979.<ref name="rjsgrp"/>

Saykally and his students developed [[velocity modulation spectroscopy]] to study gaseous ions, including the hydronium (H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>), hydroxide (OH<sup>−</sup>), and ammonium (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) ions.<ref name="jphysa">{{Cite journal |last1=Wilson |first1=Kevin R. |last2=Gruebele |first2=Martin |last3=Ziurys |first3=Lucy |date=January 23, 2025 |title=A Tribute to Richard J. Saykally |journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry A |volume=129 |issue=3 |pages=643–644 |doi=10.1021/acs.jpca.4c08425}}</ref> His group applied terahertz [[Rotational–vibrational spectroscopy|laser vibration-rotation-tunneling spectroscopy]] to map the hydrogen bonding in water clusters and develop accurate potentials for liquid water.<ref name="jphysa"/> His early research also determined the structure and spectroscopy of small carbon clusters.<ref name="nas_profile"/> 

His laboratory shifted toward condensed-phase systems in the early 2000s.<ref name="jphysa"/> Saykally used nonlinear optical methods and [[X-ray spectroscopy]] of liquid [[microjets]] to evaluate the solvation of ions at air-water and oil-water interfaces.<ref name="jphysa"/> His recent work implements nonlinear techniques at free-electron lasers to analyze graphite surfaces.<ref name="jphysa"/>

== Honors and awards ==
Saykally is an elected member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] and the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]].<ref name="nas_profile"/><ref name="amacad">{{Cite web |title=Richard James Saykally |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/richard-james-saykally |publisher=[[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] |access-date=2026-07-22}}</ref> He is a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]], the [[Optical Society of America]], and the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]].<ref name="ucb_profile"/> 

The U.S. Department of Energy awarded Saykally the [[Ernest Orlando Lawrence Award]] in 2004 for his development of velocity modulation spectroscopy.<ref name="doe_lawrence">{{Cite web |title=Berkeley Lab Scientist Wins E.O. Lawrence Award |url=https://www2.lbl.gov/Publications/Currents/Archive/Oct-01-2004.html |publisher=[[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]] |date=October 1, 2004 |access-date=2026-07-22}}</ref> The [[American Chemical Society]] recognized him with the [[Irving Langmuir Award]] in Chemical Physics in 2000, the [[Peter Debye Award]] in Physical Chemistry in 2009, and the E. Bright Wilson Award in Spectroscopy in 2018.<ref name="ucb_profile"/> 

The Royal Society of Chemistry awarded him the [[Bourke Award]] in 1992, the Centenary Medal in 2000, and the Faraday Lectureship Prize in 2012.<ref name="ucb_profile"/> He held the [[Hinshelwood Lectureship]] at [[University of Oxford|Oxford University]] in 2006 and the Inaugural [[Solvay Chair in Chemistry]] at the [[Solvay Institutes]] in 2008.<ref name="ucb_profile"/> He received the Helmholtz International Fellow Award in 2018.<ref name="helmholtz">{{Cite web |title=Professor Richard Saykally receives Helmholtz International Fellow award |url=https://chemistry.berkeley.edu/news/professor-richard-saykally-receives-helmholtz-international-fellow-award |publisher=[[University of California, Berkeley]] |date=2018 |access-date=2026-07-22}}</ref>
